findings.description: Kumasawa’s お迎え待ち is a death euphemism in her self-deprecating reply: the decrepit woman awaiting her own final summons is welcoming the guests. WH makes her merely the woman waiting to greet them. The repeated お迎え loses the collision of guest pickup and death’s arrival, following Rudolf’s one-foot-in-the-coffin joke.

棺桶に半分足突っ込んだ人がはしゃいじゃいけねぇぜ」
「若い方とじゃれるのが、何よりの若返りの薬ですよ。
ほっほっほ！」
「熊沢さんが迎えに来るなんて珍しいじゃない。
どういう風の吹き回しかしらぁ？
用事を頼まれるといつも腰痛になるあなたが。
くすくす」
「ほっほっほ、絵羽さまは相変わらず手厳しゅうございます。
急なお買い物がありましたもので、そのついでに皆様のお迎えをしようと思いまして。
もっともお迎え待ちの老いぼれのお迎えでは景気もお悪いでしょうが。
ほっほっほ…！」
さらりと嫌味を言う絵羽伯母さんだが、熊沢の婆ちゃんはさすがに年季が入ってる。
さらりと涼しげに受け流して見せるぜ。

findings.sourceReading: The greeting sense belongs to お迎えでは; お迎え待ちの老いぼれ qualifies the old woman as awaiting death.
findings.alternative: Both occurrences use the same greeting word, making a literal greeting reading tempting. The coffin remark and 老いぼれ make the death euphemism operative; WH retains decrepitude but loses that double meaning.

findings.description: Rosa has remembered last year’s promise and bought the tea. Kumasawa is touched not only by that remembered promise but by Rosa bringing a gift even for a servant. WH says ‘Whether or not Kumasawa ... remembered’ the promise. It assigns the remembering to the recipient and replaces the additive ばかりか construction with uncertainty.

contexts.WH: Whether or not Kumasawa baa-chan remembered this year-old promise, she seemed deeply touched by the fact that someone would bring a gift to a simple servant like her.
contexts.MG:
"You just seem to get more and more lively.
Oh, that's right, here you are.
It's the tea I told you about before.
Look, I bought you some.
Please do try it later on."
Aunt Rosa took a souvenir bag out from her suitcase.
To think that she remembered a promise that she'd apparently made last year and faithfully bought it.
...This sort of thoughtfulness was just like Aunt Rosa.
She wasn't the kind of person who would forget or break a promise.
Kumasawa baa-chan seemed deeply touched, not only that Aunt Rosa had remembered this year-old promise, but that she would bring a gift to a simple servant like her.
contexts.UP:
"You just seem to get more and more lively.
Oh, that's right, here you are.
It's the tea I was talking about before.
Look, I bought some.
Please do try it later on."
Auntie Rosa showed her the souvenir bag she'd taken out of her suitcase.

contexts.note: Both correctly assign remembered promise to Rosa and retain not only/but gift to servant. WH recipient/uncertainty error no longer applies; do not copy it into error counts.

findings.sourceReading: The preceding narration explicitly identifies Rosa as the person faithfully remembering and fulfilling her promise. Kumasawa is the experiencer of 感激, while the remembered promise and gift are the reasons.
findings.alternative: The Japanese topic remains Kumasawa and the embedded subject is unstated, so the raw clause can tempt a subject error. Even on that reading, ばかりか is not ‘whether or not’; the continuous context establishes Rosa’s thoughtfulness.

findings.description: Jessica says the boat has four high-performance propellers. WH describes ‘four-base high efficiency propellers,’ treating the machine counter 基 as part of the apparatus description and losing the explicit count of four individual propellers.

contexts.WH: "Anyway, it's the captain's pride and joy, and it's a kinda modded high-speed boat.  Seems he tinkers with big parts of it.  He was bragging about how he attached four-base high efficiency propellers to it so that he could break 40 knots or something like that.  I just remember how he's always bragging."

He bragged to me so much I ended up memorizing it."

The captain said that since he lost a speed contest with a foreign fishing boat a long time ago, he became obsessed with modding.

contexts.note: MG retains four-base; UP explicitly four propellers. Count, speed and reported captain boast considered together.

findings.sourceReading: ４基 counts four installed units; it does not describe a four-base design. The exceeding-40-knots boast remains separately expressed.
findings.alternative: Readers might guess four-base implies four, but it supplies no intelligible count or established apparatus configuration. The numerical statement in Japanese is straightforward.

findings.description: George says his parents repeatedly urged him about entrance exams when those exams were approaching. WH says ‘When I was slacking off during exams,’ inventing neglect and moving the pressure into the exam period. This changes his account of his parents’ insistence and his own younger conduct.

findings.description: After George expresses gratitude for his parents’ pressure, Battler calls him 人間が出来てる, praising his mature character. WH has ‘George-aniki can be human too,’ which reads as discovering human vulnerability or ordinary humanity rather than admiring maturity. It breaks Battler’s impressed response to George’s gratitude.

findings.description: Kumasawa asks whether Battler has not yet returned to the parental home. WH asks whether he still ‘cannot return,’ introducing an obstacle or inability. His reply describes occasional visits and belongings still at the previous house; subsequent narration says he has had to return after his maternal grandparents died.

contexts.WH: "Battler-san, you still cannot return to your home?"
contexts.MG:
"Battler-san, have you still not returned to your parents' home?"
"...Well, I kinda go back now and then.
I've got lots of clothes and stuff left at the house I was living in until recently."
"......Uu-?
Battler has two houses?"
"Uh,
.........hmmm.
......Something like that."
"Why?
Why do you have two houses?
Uu-?
Uu-?"
Only Maria, who couldn't really grasp the situation, voiced this naive question.
However, the others just shot nervous glances at me, choosing not to respond even though they knew the answer.
"Maria!
Look, you can see the harbor now...!
Look, over there!
Can you see it?!"
"Uu-!
Saw the harbor, saw the harbor!"
Apparently, Jessica was trying to be nice by changing the subject.
......Ah, well.
I'd rather not talk about it if I can help it, but it's uncomfortable to have it treated like some kind of weird taboo.
......I don't mind it that much myself anymore.
I may be a member of the Ushiromiya family,
but the truth is that, for these last six years, I've been living with my grandparents on my late mother's side, and I've even been using her family name.
When those grandparents passed away one after the other, I basically had no choice but to go back and live with the old bastard.
Don't get me wrong.
I didn't just run away from home or anything like that.
The only one at fault here is my dad.
......I don't really blame Kyrie-san.
Being able to hold that old bastard's reins and ride him out is no mean feat. ...Still, the way that old bastard betrayed my mom...
......Well, unfortunately, I still haven't fully gotten over that.

findings.sourceReading: まだ ... 戻られておられない asks about the state of not yet having returned; the honorific passive-form 戻られる is not an inability construction.
findings.alternative: The awkward family circumstances explain delicacy, but they do not establish a prohibition or inability to return. The English question introduces one as its premise.

The MangaGamer and PS3 witnesses are not independently certified retail extractions.

findings.description: Jessica agrees with Battler’s proposed natural cause, but then states that the shrine disappeared this summer. WH carries uncertainty into the separate date statement: ‘It probably disappeared during the summer.’ Readers lose the definite seasonal anchor supplied by the island resident, independently of whether the proposed cause is true.

It was a small crag, so it probably got worn away over time."

But they say-"

contexts.UP:
"Maybe they were washed away by the waves or something?
It was a small crag, it probably got brittle because of its exposure."
"I think so too.
It actually disappeared during the summer.
Apparently—"
"A huge lightning bolt fell one evening and smashed the shrine, or some such...
......The fishermen whisper that it must undoubtedly be an ominous sign, to have a thunderbolt fall upon our tutelary god.
...Lightning begone, lightning begone..."
contexts.note: Both give unhedged summer disappearance separately from agreement with wave explanation. WH probable-date error gone. MG last summer refers most recent summer in October setting, not necessarily previous calendar year.

findings.sourceReading: 私もそうだと思ってる qualifies agreement with the wave explanation. なくなっちゃったのはこの夏のことなんだよ then asserts the season without a probability marker.
findings.alternative: The prior と思ってる concerns the proposed cause; extending it over the date conflates separate assertions. Kumasawa’s subsequent hearsay explanation does not make Jessica’s date a guess.

findings.description: Jessica’s 何でもよぅ introduces something heard, continued by Kumasawa’s だとか report of lightning destroying the shrine. WH has Jessica dismiss it with ‘Whatever,’ then makes Kumasawa propose ‘Or perhaps’ lightning. The reported account becomes an alternative she is speculating about rather than an account circulating independently of her suggestion.

contexts.note: MG they say / UP apparently and or some such preserve reported lightning account, rather than proposed speculative alternative. Fishermen whispering omen remains distinct from verified cause.

findings.sourceReading: 何でも and だとか mark hearsay; they do not certify lightning as fact. The following fishermen’s ominous interpretation is another explicitly attributed report.
findings.alternative: The English still reports fishermen’s beliefs about an omen, and Japanese hearsay is uncertain. But uncertainty about a reported event is different from inventing a possible explanation; the original neither asserts certainty nor frames a personal alternative hypothesis.
